$comment: THE COMPATIBILITY MATRIX (Task 043B, R3).
Three cells, and the reason there are three is that each one catches a
different release-engineering mistake:
old-api-new-db   The previous release's IMAGE against the CURRENT schema.
This is the rollback. It is the cell that is easiest to
forget, and the first one that becomes impossible to run:
once the previous image is dequeued from the registry and
the previous schema head is gone, this cell can never be
produced again. A matrix that is refreshed after that
point is a matrix that has quietly lost its hardest test.
new-api-old-db   The CANDIDATE against the PREVIOUS schema. This is what
catches a new NOT NULL column with no default: the schema
diff calls it additive, the candidate boots fine against its
own schema, and the failure only appears in the window
between the code deploying and the migration running - which
is the window the migration Job exists to close, and the one
nobody rehearses.
new-api-new-db   The ordinary case. Recorded so that a failure in the two
hard cells can be attributed: if the candidate fails
everywhere, the candidate is broken, not the window.
PROBES - THREE, NOT ONE
1. GET /health, and the MIGRATION-CURRENCY CHECK WITHIN IT. Not the
aggregate code. /health/ready is 200 or 503 over PostgreSQL, object
storage, the broker, Redis and migration currency together, so a matrix
keyed on it is keyed on whether a bucket happens to be reachable. /health
answers the same aggregate AND names each check, so the verdict this
matrix is about can be read on its own. 'absent' is a real answer and is
distinct from 'Unhealthy': a build that predates the check is not a build
whose check says the schema is wrong.
2. POST /api/v1/projects. The WRITE is not optional. A new NOT NULL
column with no default breaks the INSERT, and a read of the project the
harness just created succeeds happily - so a read-only matrix proves
half of what it claims.
3. GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/workspace - the task's 'one workspace read'.
Every probe path is checked by scripts/check-rollout-window.mjs against the
COMMITTED OpenAPI document, so a probe whose route was renamed is a gate
finding rather than a 404 read as 'no rows'. The document puts the version
prefix in servers[0].url and the route in paths, and the gate accounts for
that. The hosting endpoints (/health, /version) are exempt because they are
registered outside the document on purpose: they are AllowAnonymous, and a
document that listed them would advertise unauthenticated paths.
`expect` is DATA, and the gate compares the recorded run against it
Each cell declares the statuses that constitute a pass, and the gate reads
them from here rather than from the run. A run cannot pass by declaring its
own expectations, and a cell that quietly acquires a new expectation is a
reviewed diff.
Note the expectation of new-api-old-db: migration-currency Unhealthy,
deliberately. See its `readinessNote`.
`unavailable` - A DECLARED, DATED, REASONED EXEMPTION
A cell that cannot be run, named, with the reason, the condition that
unblocks it, the risk being accepted, and a review date. The gate REQUIRES
all five and fails when any is missing, when the `reviewBy` has passed, or
when the entry names a cell that is not in the matrix.
This is not a way to make a red matrix green, and the difference is worth
stating. A suppression hides a failure. A declaration records that a specific
check cannot be performed, says exactly why in words a reviewer can check,
and stops being accepted on a date. The gate also PRINTS every exemption, so
an exemption can never be invisible in a green run.
HOW TO RUN IT: bash deploy/rollout/compat-smoke.sh
It writes the run here, preserving this block; the gate decides whether the
record is acceptable.

probes: GET /health -> the migration-currency check reports Healthy
matrix.proves: the previous release's code tolerates the expanded schema, which is the precondition for the code-only rollback in docs/runbooks/rollback.md

matrix.readinessNote: Unhealthy is the CORRECT answer here, and this cell is what proves it. MigrationCurrencyCheck deliberately reports a build that is AHEAD of the schema as not-ready, so a pod never takes traffic before its own migration has run. Expecting Healthy in this cell would have required disabling that check, or producing a permanent failure that everybody learned to ignore. Note that the gate reads the migration-currency check ON ITS OWN rather than the aggregate /health code: the aggregate also covers object storage, and a matrix keyed on it is keyed on whether a bucket happens to be reachable.
probes: GET /health -> the migration-currency check reports Unhealthy because the build is ahead of the schema
matrix.proves: the candidate tolerates the schema it is not shipped with; a new column is nullable or defaulted, so the candidate is not waiting on its own migration to boot

probes: GET /health -> the migration-currency check reports Healthy
matrix.proves: the candidate works at all, so a failure in the two window cells is attributable to the window rather than to the candidate

unavailable.reason: THERE IS NO PREVIOUS RELEASE. This repository has never been released, so there is no previous product to point a previous IMAGE at. Building one from 'the commit before the newest migration' produces something that is not a release: that tree has no WorkspaceController, no /health or /version endpoints and no MigrationCurrencyCheck, and its API answers 404 on /api/v1/me, /api/v1/dashboard, /api/v1/notifications and on the workspace route. A cell that 'passed' against that build would be measuring a different product, and a cell that failed would be blamed on the schema.
unavailable.unblockedWhen: the first tagged release exists. From then on the cell runs for real: build the previous tag's image, apply the current head, probe. This is why the cell is declared rather than quietly dropped - it is the cell the FIRST release after a change will need, and it is the first one that becomes impossible once the previous image is dequeued.
unavailable.riskAccepted: Until the first release there is no previous product to be incompatible with, so a code-only rollback has nothing to roll back TO. The rollback MECHANISM is separately rehearsed on a real cluster by deploy/rollout/rehearse-rollback.sh and recorded in deploy/rollout/rollback-rehearsal.json; that is the part that can be quietly wrong.
